<<The Orange Tower>>

Section 1
From her glass tower overlooking the sprawling airfield, Carolyn McCall surveyed her kingdom. It was a kingdom of vibrant orange and stark white, of 80.2 million subjects who, in the past year, had trusted her airline to carry them across the skies. The sheer volume was a record, a testament to her strategy of dominating Europe's key airports. The planes were fuller than ever. Yet, from her high vantage point, the balance sheet told a different story. Profits had tumbled by 17%, a sickening drop from £494m to £408m. A single political tremor, the Brexit vote, had sent a shockwave through the currency markets, wiping more than £100m from their earnings. To keep the passenger numbers soaring, she’d had to offer lower fares, a necessary treat to fill every last seat in what she knew was a brutal year for aviation.

Section 2
The tremors of that political earthquake continued to rattle the very foundations of her company. Brexit wasn't just a past event; it was a future challenge that required a bold, almost unthinkable, response. The rules of a new, fractured Europe dictated that the airline must be majority EU-owned to continue its unrestricted flights. This a problem, a knot that needed untangling, with the founder, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, and his dual nationality representing a significant, but insufficient, EU stake. So, a plan was forged, a gambit so audacious that many in the financial society whispered, "How could they dare?" The proposal was simple and severe: take the power to force UK shareholders to sell their stakes. It was a move that prioritized the company's operational future over individual investor loyalty, a technical solution to a political mess that felt anything but technical to those whose ownership was now at risk.

Section 3
Just as the whispers of dissent grew louder, a ray of light pierced the clouds. As the news of the difficult year broke, so too did the news of the future. Forward bookings were soaring. Shares, instead of falling, jumped by more than 5%. The market, it seemed, understood Carolyn’s ruthless logic. While other airlines had struggled and gone bankrupt, leaving a vacuum, Carolyn was going fishing. Her airline was perfectly positioned to scoop up the disillusioned customers left stranded on the tarmac. This sudden surge in revenue wasn't luck; it was the direct result of a strategy that saw weakness in the market and moved to exploit it. From her tower, Carolyn saw the path forward. The ownership issue was a mere administrative hurdle. The real story was the resilience of her orange empire and its readiness to claim the spoils of a turbulent sky.
